summaries.example: Imagine learning that the warmth of a cup of cocoa comes from tiny moving particles. The cocoa is still warm, but we now explain its warmth using something more basic. Philosophers ask whether this counts as reduction, and whether the explanation keeps everything important about warmth.
summaries.summary: Scientific reduction is the idea that something can be brought back, in an important explanatory or philosophical sense, to something more basic. For example, heat has been discussed in relation to the motion of tiny particles, and mental events have been discussed in relation to physical events. The source explains that being more basic is necessary for reduction but is not enough by itself. A strong reduction must also show the right kind of connection, such as an explanation, an identity, or a relation between theories. Philosophers have proposed several models. Ernest Nagel’s model uses derivation and bridge principles connecting the vocabularies of two theories. Structuralist models compare the structures of theories. “New Wave” models emphasize constructing a corrected version of an older theory inside a newer one and allow a range from close preservation to replacement. Mechanistic approaches explain a whole by describing the organized activities of its parts. The entry also discusses reductions involving mental properties, including type identity, token identity, multiple realization, and functional roles. It concludes that no single account has settled every question, and that reduction may mean different things in different areas of philosophy and science.
key_ideas: Reduction tries to explain one thing using something considered more basic.
A thing can depend on something deeper without being reduced to it. For example, dependence alone may not be enough.
Most reductionists think the original thing is still real, rather than simply erased.
Scientists and philosophers disagree about whether reductions connect theories, models, properties, or mechanisms.
Some reductions keep the older ideas almost completely; others replace or correct them.
A reduction may be useful even when a perfect, complete reduction is not possible.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reduction helps us ask how different kinds of knowledge fit together. It can clarify connections between physics and chemistry, psychology and neuroscience, or a whole machine and its parts. It also helps us notice that explaining something through its parts does not automatically make the larger thing unreal or unimportant. Understanding the debate teaches us to distinguish explanation, dependence, identity, and replacement instead of treating them as the same idea.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical idea that one thing can be understood through something more basic or fundamental.
A theory that says a higher-level thing is not something extra beyond a more basic thing, though it may still be real.
A set of connected ideas used to explain part of the world.
A statement or rule that connects ideas from two different theories.
The parts and activities that work together to make a larger thing do what it does.

questions_to_think_about: If warmth is explained by moving particles, is warmth still a real feature?
Can two different explanations both be useful without one reducing to the other?
When does replacing an old theory count as reduction, and when is it just replacement?
Why might scientists study the parts of a mechanism instead of only looking for one big law?

summaries.example: Suppose a scientist explains a gas law using the motion of molecules. A simple version of reduction would derive the older gas law from molecular theory. But the fit may require limiting conditions, approximations, or corrections. Philosophers therefore ask whether the older law has been reduced, merely approximated, or replaced—and whether the gas law remains a real and useful description.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of scientific reduction studies when one theory, model, property, or phenomenon can be brought into an important relation with another that is more basic. The source distinguishes this technical idea from the everyday meaning of “reduce.” Reduction may be conservative: the reduced phenomenon remains real, although it is understood through a base. It may also be eliminativist, where the newer account replaces the older entity, though the entry treats that as a terminological issue rather than the standard case. In philosophy of science, the central question has often concerned theory reduction. Nagel’s model requires the reduced theory to follow from the reducing theory, with bridge principles where vocabularies differ. Problems arise because derivability alone can make reduction reflexive, permit relations involving inconsistent theories, and fail to capture asymmetry. It can also seem too narrow for fields that rely on models rather than complete theories. Structuralist approaches compare formal structures, but critics worry that purely structural similarity lacks a connection to what the theories are about. New Wave approaches construct a corrected analogue of the older theory within the newer framework and treat reduction as ranging from close retention to replacement. In philosophy of mind, type identity, token identity, local reduction, disjunctive kinds, and functional reduction offer different ways to relate mental and physical descriptions. The entry also examines supervenience, realization, part-whole explanation, mechanisms, explanation, and metaphysical grounding. Its overall conclusion is pluralistic and cautious: reduction remains an important family of ideas, but its exact meaning and scope are unsettled.
key_ideas: Reduction has both ontological and explanatory interpretations: it may concern what exists, how something is explained, or how theories are related.
Nagel’s influential model treats reduction as derivation of one theory from another, sometimes with bridge principles and additional conditions.
Critics argue that Nagelian reduction is too narrow, too formal, or unable to handle correction, approximation, models, and scientific practice adequately.
Structuralist models compare theory structures, while New Wave models use corrected theoretical analogues and a continuum from preservation to replacement.
Multiple realization challenges simple type-identity theories, but local reductions, disjunctive kinds, and functional sub-types are proposed responses.
Mechanistic explanation accounts for a whole through the organized activities and interactions of its components, but philosophers disagree about whether this is reductive.
summaries.why_it_matters: Reduction is a test case for larger questions about scientific unity, explanation, emergence, and the relation between levels of reality. It affects how we understand whether biology can be connected to chemistry, whether psychology can be related to neuroscience, and whether a whole is fully understood by describing its components. The debate also shows why formal derivation, empirical discovery, identity, dependence, and replacement should not be casually identified. Different sciences may require different models, and attention to actual scientific explanations can challenge overly simple pictures of a single hierarchy with one final basic level.

important_terms.definition: A relation in which one entity, property, theory, or model is understood through another that is treated as more basic, prior, or fundamental.
Reduction understood as a relation between representations such as theories, models, or concepts.
Reduction understood as a relation among real-world entities, properties, events, or mechanisms.
A proposed connection between the vocabulary or subject matter of two theories; its status may be logical, conventional, or empirical.
The view that a property or kind at one level is identical with a property or kind at another level.
The view that each particular occurrence is physical, while the higher-level types or properties need not be identical.
The possibility that one higher-level kind can be produced by different lower-level physical kinds.
An account of a property in terms of the role it plays in a system, such as a causal or computational role.

questions_to_think_about: Does deriving an older law from a newer theory show that the older law has been reduced, or only that it works under special conditions?
If a mental property is realized by different physical properties in different organisms, can it still be reduced to the physical?
Why might supervenience be necessary for reduction yet insufficient for it?
Should replacement of a theory, such as the removal of an old theoretical entity, count as reduction?
Can a theory be reduced if the connection between the two theories is discovered empirically rather than known in advance?

summaries.example: Think about a fitness tracker. It may describe your activity as “running,” while its sensors record movements and signals. One philosopher might ask whether running can be explained entirely in sensor language. Another might say that the sensor readings realize the activity without making the useful idea of running disappear. The disagreement is similar to debates about whether psychology reduces to neuroscience.
summaries.summary: Scientific reduction is a family of views about how one level of description or theory relates to another that is more basic. The source begins with a broad idea: if x reduces to y, then y is in some sense prior, fundamental, or able to explain x. But this condition is not sufficient. Reductionists usually defend a conservative realism: the reduced phenomenon remains real, even though it is not something extra beyond the reducing base. In some cases, however, an old entity is eliminated when a new theory replaces it. The philosophy of science has focused especially on reductions between successive theories, such as relations discussed between mechanics and relativity or chemistry and atomic physics. Nagel’s influential model treats reduction as a logical relation: the reducing theory, together with bridge laws, should yield the reduced theory. Critics point out that this can be too narrow, because science often uses models, approximations, and partial reductions. They also raise formal problems, including the fact that derivability by itself does not guarantee asymmetry. Structuralist models respond by treating theories as organized structures and comparing their models. New Wave models construct a revised version of the older theory within the newer framework and place cases along a range from smooth retention to rough replacement. In the philosophy of mind, type identity says mental and physical kinds are the same; token identity says each particular mental event is physical without requiring identity of the kinds. Multiple realization motivates local reductions, disjunctive kinds, and functional approaches. Mechanistic explanation adds another possibility: explaining a system through the coordinated activities of its parts. The entry ends by stressing unresolved ties
key_ideas: Reduction can concern theories and models, but it can also concern real properties, events, or mechanisms.
A thing being more fundamental is required by many accounts of reduction, but that alone does not prove reduction.
Nagel’s model says that a reduced theory should follow from a reducing theory, sometimes with bridge laws linking their vocabularies.
Critics of Nagel argue that this picture can be too formal and may not fit corrections, approximations, models, or how scientists actually discover connections.
Structuralist accounts focus on similarities between theory structures; New Wave accounts allow reductions to vary from close preservation to replacement.
In philosophy of mind, multiple realization challenges the idea that every mental kind matches one physical kind, although local or functional reductions may still be possible.
summaries.why_it_matters: Questions about reduction influence how we understand scientific progress and the relation between fields. They also shape debates about whether psychology has its own legitimate concepts even if every mental event has a physical basis. Studying the topic helps distinguish several claims that can sound alike: that one thing is caused by another, depends on another, is identical with another, is explained by another, or is replaced by another. Those distinctions matter when deciding what a scientific explanation really accomplishes.

important_terms.definition: The idea that one thing can be brought back to, or explained in terms of, something more basic.
The position that higher-level things do not exist as something extra beyond a more basic level, while usually treating them as real.
A connection between the terms or laws of two theories that helps one theory relate to the other.
A description or mathematical structure used to represent how a system works; it may be less complete than a full theory.
The possibility that different lower-level physical arrangements can produce the same higher-level kind.
A property described by the role it plays, such as receiving inputs and producing outputs, rather than by one particular material.
A way of explaining what a whole does by describing the organized actions and interactions of its parts.
A relation of dependence in which something is treated as more basic or prior, without automatically being identical to it.

questions_to_think_about: If two different machines can perform the same function, is the function identical with one machine’s physical parts?
Does a newer theory reduce an older one if it explains only some of the older theory’s cases?
Why might a useful model fail to count as a complete scientific theory?
Is explaining a whole by its parts always a form of reduction?
What is the difference between saying that one property depends on another and saying that the two properties are identical?
